title: Vijayabahu I expels the Cholas
summary: From his base in Ruhuna, Vijayabahu I drove the Cholas out of Rajarata and made Polonnaruwa his capital. He restored the Buddhist sangha by bringing ordained monks from Ramanna (Lower Burma).

evidence.description: Vijayabahu's campaigns and reign.
Inscriptions of Vijayabahu I and the Chola-period records.

title: Reign of Parakramabahu I
summary: Parakramabahu I reunified the island and unified the Buddhist fraternities under the Mahavihara. He undertook vast irrigation works including the Parakrama Samudra and sent expeditions to South India and to Ramanna (Burma). Polonnaruwa reached its architectural peak in his reign.

evidence.description: The Culavamsa's extended treatment of Parakramabahu I.
Ancient City of Polonnaruwa, World Heritage inscription 1982.
Galvihara inscription recording the reform of the sangha.

historiography: The Culavamsa's account was written as royal panegyric. Liyanagamage and others argue that the cost of his wars and building works helped bring about Polonnaruwa's later decline.

title: Nissanka Malla and the Galpota inscription
summary: Nissanka Malla was a ruler of Kalinga origin who left more inscriptions than any other Sri Lankan king. The 'stone book' (Galpota) at Polonnaruwa sets out his ideology of kingship, including the claim that only Buddhists of the Kalinga line were fit to rule.

evidence.description: Galpota and other Nissanka Malla inscriptions.
Brief account of his reign.

title: Invasion of Kalinga Magha
summary: The Culavamsa describes the invader Magha, with Kerala and Tamil soldiers, ruling harshly at Polonnaruwa. Sinhala political centres moved to the south-west, and the Rajarata hydraulic heartland went into long-term decline.

evidence.description: Account of Magha's invasion and rule.
Analysis of the decline of Polonnaruwa and the drift to the south-west.

historiography: How destructive Magha's rule was, how far it caused the 'drift to the south-west', and whether he founded the Jaffna kingdom are all debated. Other proposed causes include malaria, the cost of war, and irrigation that had become unsustainable.

perspectives.label: Chronicle
perspectives.view: A catastrophic invasion that destroyed the Buddhist order in Rajarata.

perspectives.label: Revisionist
perspectives.view: Decline had several causes and had already begun; the chronicle's account is rhetorical.

title: Dambadeniya and Parakramabahu II
summary: From Dambadeniya, Parakramabahu II drove back Magha's forces, recovered the tooth and bowl relics, and repelled the invasion of Chandrabhanu of Tambralinga. His court was a centre of Sinhala and Pali literature.

evidence.description: Parakramabahu II's reign.
Political history of the Dambadeniya period.

title: Yapahuwa rock fortress and the loss of the Tooth Relic
summary: Bhuvanekabahu I fortified Yapahuwa, whose ornate stairway housed the tooth relic. After his death a Pandyan army took the relic to South India, and Parakramabahu III later recovered it by negotiation.

evidence.description: Yapahuwa period and the Pandyan seizure of the relic.

title: Rise of the Jaffna kingdom (Aryacakravartis)
dateNote: The kingdom's founding date and founder are debated.
summary: A Tamil kingdom ruled by the Aryacakravarti dynasty, centred on Nallur, controlled the Jaffna peninsula and at its height the north-west pearl fisheries. Ibn Battuta met its ruler at Puttalam in 1344.

evidence.description: Ibn Battuta's meeting with 'Ayri Shakarwati', who ruled the pearl coast.
Discussion of the background to the northern Tamil polity.
Later Tamil chronicle tradition (Yalpana Vaipava Malai, 18th c.) summarised in standard histories.
The kingdom's own later chronicle tradition.

historiography: Some historians tie the origins to Magha's invasion and others to Pandyan expansion. The main Tamil chronicle, the Yalpana Vaipava Malai, is late (18th century), so contemporary inscriptions and foreign accounts carry the most weight. The primary sources for this entry need expanding.

title: Ibn Battuta's pilgrimage to Adam's Peak
summary: The Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta landed at Battala (Puttalam), was received by the Aryacakravarti ruler, and climbed Sri Pada, which Muslims venerate as the site of Adam's footprint. He then travelled south to Dinawar (Dondra) and Galle.

evidence.description: Ibn Battuta's account of Ceylon.

title: The Gampola kingdom and its temples
summary: With the capital at Gampola, kings of this period built the Lankatilaka and Gadaladeniya temples, which mix Sinhala, South Indian and Vijayanagara architectural styles. Real power often lay with the Alagakkonara ministers.

evidence.description: Lankatilaka and Gadaladeniya temples; political narrative.
Temple inscriptions of the Gampola period.

title: Zheng He's trilingual inscription at Galle
summary: A stone slab erected by the Ming admiral Zheng He records offerings in Chinese to the Buddha, in Tamil to Tenavarai Nayanar, and in Persian to Allah. It was discovered in Galle in 1911 and is now in the Colombo National Museum.

evidence.description: Edition of the inscription.
Context of the Ming voyages.

title: Ming forces capture Vira Alakesvara
summary: On a return voyage, Zheng He's forces fought the ruler Vira Alakesvara and took him to Nanjing as a captive. Ming records then describe the Ming court's role in installing a successor, and the episode shows the military side of the 'treasure voyages'.

evidence.description: Ming Shilu and other Chinese records, analysed as evidence of Ming military intervention.
Sri Lankan political context.

title: Parakramabahu VI unifies the island from Kotte
summary: Parakramabahu VI ruled from Kotte for over fifty years and was the last king to bring the whole island under one rule. His forces, led by Sapumal Kumaraya, conquered Jaffna around 1450. His reign was a high point of Sinhala literature, including the sandesa poems and the work of Totagamuve Sri Rahula.

evidence.description: Political history of Kotte to 1521.
Culavamsa account of the reign.

title: Emergence of the Kandyan kingdom
dateNote: The founding date and first king (Senasammata Vikramabahu) are approximate.
summary: In the late 15th century the hill country around Senkadagala broke away from Kotte under Senasammata Vikramabahu. It became the core of the Kandyan kingdom, which stayed independent of European rule until 1815.

evidence.description: Narrative of Kandy's emergence.

historiography: Sources for Kandy's origins are sparse and late. Dates for the first independent ruler vary between the 1460s and 1470s, and Kandy's status as a separate kingdom (rather than a Kotte dependency) was only consolidated in the 16th century.

title: Velaikkara inscription: Tamil guardians of the Tooth Relic
summary: A Tamil inscription records that the Velaikkara mercenaries undertook to protect the Tooth Relic temple at Polonnaruwa, built under Vijayabahu I. It shows South Indian soldiers acting as guardians of the Buddhist palladium.

evidence.description: Edition of the Velaikkara slab inscription.

title: Nainativu Tamil inscription of Parakramabahu I
summary: A Tamil royal edict of Parakramabahu I regulating foreign merchants and shipwrecked cargo at the northern port of Uratturai (Kayts). It shows royal control of trade and the use of Tamil in royal administration.

evidence.description: Discussion of the inscription.

title: Portuguese sack of Devinuwara
summary: A Portuguese raiding force destroyed the celebrated temple of Upulvan/Vishnu at Devinuwara, one of the great shrines of the Indian Ocean world.

evidence.description: Portuguese account of the raid.
Earlier description of the temple's splendour.

title: Destruction of Koneswaram
summary: Captain-General Constantino de Sá de Noronha demolished the Koneswaram temple on Swami Rock and built a fort with its stones, one of several major Hindu temples destroyed by the Portuguese.

evidence.description: Portuguese account.
Antiquity of the shrine in Tevaram literature.

title: Senarat resettles Muslims in the east
summary: After the Portuguese expelled Muslims from the lowlands, the Kandyan king Senarat is said to have resettled several thousand of them in the Batticaloa region. Tradition places the origins of many eastern Muslim communities here.

evidence.description: Muslim settlement and the Kandyan kingdom.

title: Medieval Sinhala coinage: the kahavanu and massa
summary: Gold kahavanu and copper massa coins bearing the standing and seated "king" figure and royal names in Nagari (e.g. Sri Lankesvara, Parakramabahu). They circulated widely and were imitated in South India.

evidence.description: Typology of the "Ceylon man" coinage.
